title: A Harvest for the Bell
premise: Cyrus Marchetti, a hospice nurse who has spent seven years rationalizing the way the dying count backwards, inherits his grandmother's farmhouse and discovers every mirror in it reflects the room one second late. The lag is not a defect but an invitation: something beneath the old well on the property was promised a harvest decades ago, and the family debt has come due. As the house seals itself against dawn, Cyrus must piece together his grandmother's bargain — made to save a daughter, at the cost of everyone who came after — while the reflections begin moving on their own. He survives only by offering the bell in the well what it truly wants: a remembered name freely given, breaking the cycle as sunrise refills the water.
about_author: Cyrus Vane spent a decade working night shifts in long-term care facilities across rural Ohio before turning to writing full-time. His fiction draws on the small, unexplainable kindnesses and terrors he witnessed among the dying.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Cyrus Marchetti works a final shift at Bellhaven Hospice, where patient Edith Wray counts backwards from thirty in her sleep and stops exactly at zero each time she flatlines. Cyrus logs it, tells himself it's Cheyne-Stokes breathing patterns. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: weary denial, the professional calm of a man who has learned not to look directly at things.

chapters.title: Letters from a Dead Woman
chapters.summary: A lawyer's letter arrives: Cyrus's estranged grandmother, Vera Marchetti, has died and left him the farmhouse in Hollow Creek — a place his mother forbade him to visit. The envelope contains a brass handbell wrapped in red thread and one instruction: never ring it after dark. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: reluctant inheritance, grief for a woman he barely knew.

chapters.title: Hollow Creek
chapters.summary: Cyrus drives out to the farmhouse, a sagging two-story surrounded by dead orchards and a capped stone well. Neighbor Ruth Calloway warns him the house 'keeps its own hours' and that Vera never let anyone stay past midnight. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: unease dressed as small-town eccentricity; first sense of belonging to something he doesn't understand.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: First night in the house. Cyrus catches his reflection in the hallway mirror raising its hand a beat after he does. He tests every mirror in the house — all of them lag by exactly one second, except the mirror over the mantel, which doesn't show him at all. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: the rationalizations begin to crack.

chapters.title: What Vera Kept
chapters.summary: Exploring the attic, Cyrus finds Vera's journals, decades of entries counting down dates, and a photograph of a little girl he's never seen — a sister his mother never mentioned. The last entry reads: 'It comes up when the well refills. I bought her time. Not enough.' POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: dread mixed with tenderness for the grandmother he misjudged.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Glass
chapters.summary: At dusk the mirrors stop lagging and start leading — showing the room a second before it happens. In the mantel mirror, Cyrus sees a small girl standing behind him. When he turns, no one. She appears again in every reflective surface, mouthing a name he can't hear. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into protectiveness.

chapters.title: Ruth's Bargain
chapters.summary: Cyrus confronts Ruth Calloway, who confesses the town's history: in 1968, Vera's daughter drowned in the well, and Vera rang the bell to call her back. Something answered wearing her voice. Every generation since owes it 'a harvest.' Ruth's own husband was taken in 1991. POV: mostly Cyrus with a Ruth flashback. Emotional beat: shared guilt, the relief of finally being believed.

chapters.title: Doors That Forget
chapters.summary: Night three. The house begins rearranging itself — hallways lengthen, doors open onto rooms from 1968, frozen mid-mourning. Cyrus finds the girl's bedroom preserved like a shrine, her diary naming the thing below as 'the Tallyman, who counts what is owed.' POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: claustrophobia; the past is physically closing in.

chapters.title: Backwards
chapters.summary: Cyrus realizes the dying count backwards because they hear it coming — the Tallyman counts down to each harvest. His phone dies, the truck won't start, and the property line at the orchard edge returns him to the front porch no matter which direction he walks. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: the trap snaps shut; panic giving way to grim resolve.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: At midnight the dry well gurgles audibly, filling with black water that rises without sound. The bell on its shelf begins to hum. In the mirrors, Cyrus watches himself from earlier that day — and then versions of himself he never lived, each one dying differently. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: vertigo of identity; what is owed may be him entirely.

chapters.title: Mother's Silence
chapters.summary: Among Vera's papers, Cyrus finds unopened letters to his mother, Lorraine — the surviving daughter, smuggled away before the debt could reach her. Reading them, Cyrus understands his mother's coldness was protection, and that his inheritance was not accidental: Vera chose him because he could hear them counting. POV: Cyrus with letters in Lorraine's voice. Emotional beat: heartbreak reframing family as both wound and shield.

chapters.title: The First Harvest
chapters.summary: The house replays 1968 around him: the drowning, the ringing of the bell, the thing climbing out with wet hair and the daughter's smile. Cyrus witnesses the original bargain — Vera promised 'a life for a life, until the debt is paid,' believing she was saving her child. POV: immersive memory sequence through Cyrus. Emotional beat: pity for Vera; the horror has a human origin.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: Edith Wray's death ripples backward: Cyrus finds his hospice logbook altered, her countdown now ending with his name after zero. The Tallyman's voice joins the mirrors, patient and bookkeeping-calm: 'Seven years you listened. You were always on the ledger.' POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: the personal stakes become mortal and undeniable.

chapters.title: Ruth Returns
chapters.summary: Ruth breaks the seal and enters the house at 2 a.m., carrying salt, iron nails, and her husband's old shotgun, refusing to let another neighbor be harvested. Together they fortify the kitchen — the one room whose mirrors were removed in 1974. POV: alternating Cyrus and Ruth. Emotional beat: solidarity; love expressed as stubborn presence.

chapters.title: What the Mirrors Want
chapters.summary: The Tallyman offers a trade through the reflections: walk to the well before dawn and only Cyrus is taken; refuse, and it takes Ruth, then Hollow Creek, then the hospice full of people who trusted him. It shows him his mother's face aging in fast-forward. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: temptation framed as mercy; duty versus love made literal.

chapters.title: The Girl's Name
chapters.summary: Deciphering the child's diary, Cyrus learns her name — Annalise — and that the Tallyman cannot take what is freely named and given back. Vera never spoke the name aloud after the bargain, fearing it would summon rather than release. The girl in the glass isn't hunting Cyrus; she's been trying to tell him this all along. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: revelation as compassion; the ghost is an ally.

chapters.title: Salt and Static
chapters.summary: Pre-dawn siege. The house fights back — mirrors multiply on walls that shouldn't hold them, the flooded well overflows up the stairs, and Ruth is dragged toward a reflection. Cyrus cuts her free with the red thread from the bell, learning the thread binds, not decorates. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: desperate teamwork; cost paid in blood and certainty.

chapters.title: Ring the Bell
chapters.summary: Cyrus understands the final mechanism: the bell must be rung after dark by someone who knows the truth — that's why Vera forbade it, knowing an ignorant ringer feeds the debt. At 5:12 a.m., holding Annalise's diary, he walks to the well and rings the bell once, deliberately, calling the Tallyman up to face a witness instead of a victim. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: courage as chosen vulnerability; the climax begins.

chapters.title: The Tallyman
chapters.summary: It rises from the well as a tall figure of counted things — coins, teeth, names stitched into its skin — wearing Vera's face above the collar. It demands the harvest. Cyrus speaks Annalise's name aloud and gives her back: not a soul taken, but a memory returned, dissolving the original theft. The Tallyman's ledger burns blank. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: confrontation resolved not by force but by restitution; love against duty fulfilled.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: As light hits the water, the well drains clean, the mirrors return to honest time, and the house exhales. Annalise appears once in the mantel mirror — smiling, aged as she would have been — and mouths thank you before the glass shows only morning. Ruth sits with Cyrus on the porch as the orchards, impossibly, bud. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: exhausted grace; belonging earned.

chapters.title: What We Owe the Living
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Cyrus stays in Hollow Creek, training as the town's visiting nurse for its dying. He calls his mother and reads her Vera's letters aloud; she weeps, then asks if she can come home. The bell hangs silent by the door, kept not out of fear but remembrance. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: reconciliation; memory as inheritance rather than burden.

chapters.title: A Harvest for the Bell
chapters.summary: Final chapter, years on: Cyrus tends a dying man who begins counting backwards — but this time Cyrus holds his hand and counts with him, down to zero, and nothing answers. On the mantel, the bell rings once, softly, on its own: not a summons, but a salute. Some debts, the last line suggests, are paid forward. POV: Cyrus. Emotional beat: quiet closure; horror transmuted into vigil, love outlasting duty.
